title: A Look Back at One Year of GENIUS Implementation
date_evidence: BLOG POST # A Look Back at One Year of GENIUS Implementation July 20, 2026
key_claim: The OCC expects most stablecoin issuers to hold between $6 million and $25 million in capital under its risk-based approach, versus reserve-based state money-transmission requirements that can exceed $300 million for the largest issuers; CSBS calls for a reserve-based requirement of roughly 0.5% of assets.
frame_summary: Argues GENIUS implementation is broadly under way but that the OCC has muddled stablecoin rules with an aggressive expansion of national trust charter powers beyond the National Bank Act, leaving issuers lightly capitalised relative to state standards.
verbatim_quote: The OCC expects that under its risk-based approach, most issuers will maintain between $6 million and $25 million in capital.
verbatim_list: That level would represent a sharp decrease from the reserve-based capital levels required by state money transmission laws, which can rise above $300 million for the largest issuers.

The OCC should adopt a reserve-based capital metric like the one successfully required by states to date, which would establish a capital requirement of roughly 0.5% of assets for the largest issuers.

This contradiction is especially concerning because it is part of a broader effort by the OCC to aggressively expand the powers of national trust charters beyond the limits established in the National Bank Act.

Legislation in Georgia, Florida, and Delaware enacts GENIUS-like requirements into state law, while legislation in Alabama and Maryland creates a licensing and application framework and then grants the regulator authority to implement GENIUS Act compliant rules.
notes: CSBS is the nationwide organisation of state banking regulators; classified Tier 2 (institutional association) rather than Tier 1 because the post is analytical commentary, not a rule or dataset. title: What the OCC's Wise and Bunq Denials Mean for FinTech Bank Charters
key_claim: The OCC denied Wise's proposed national trust bank in July and Bunq's proposed national bank in August on compliance, capital and management grounds, while granting Upstart preliminary conditional approval with elevated capital requirements; Payoneer's pending application would use a national trust bank to issue and manage a dollar stablecoin.
frame_summary: Argues the Wise and Bunq denials show the OCC pricing US bank readiness into fintech charters rather than turning against them, with the Upstart approval as the counter-case and a deep digital-asset pipeline still pending.
verbatim_quote: For Wise, the central issue was whether a company whose U.S. payments operation already had acknowledged AML/CFT deficiencies could demonstrate that a new bank would meet the more demanding standards imposed on federally chartered institutions.
verbatim_list: But approval came with a 12% minimum Tier 1 leverage ratio and 15% total risk-based capital ratio for its first three years, restrictions on significant departures from its approved business plan, and extensive requirements covering BSA/AML, OFAC, credit, liquidity, model risk, cybersecurity and management.
Bunq proposed bringing its European digital-bank model to the United States with deposit accounts, unsecured credit cards and subscription tiers for consumers and businesses.
Its application would use a national trust bank to issue and manage a dollar stablecoin and provide stablecoin custody and payment services tied to Payoneer’s cross-border SMB network.
